keyMessage.found: Privileged and vendor paths need only a password, and no one reviews access, although staff VPN and single sign-on already work.
keyMessage.closes: Enforce MFA on administrator and vendor access to Criticality A systems, then run the first access review.

categories.whatWorksToday: Staff use single sign-on, remote access runs through VPN with no exposed remote desktop, and administrators use separate accounts.

strengths.statement: IT runs a working identity management practice that it demonstrated, a base for a formal joiner, mover, and leaver process.
IT documents identity proofing for new accounts, but the service desk does not verify identity before resets.
Staff use single sign-on, and remote access runs through VPN with no remote desktop exposed to the internet.
Administrators use separate admin accounts and a written password standard exists, but administrator numbers are not limited.

gapFindings.title: Privileged and vendor access relies on passwords alone
gapFindings.statement: CMC controls who holds an account but not how it proves identity, so its most powerful access paths have the weakest protection.

supportingFacts.fact: Administrators sign in to HIS, PACS, and Active Directory without multi-factor authentication (MFA).
Vendors connect to HIS and PACS through unattended remote tools.
Microsoft 365 has MFA for administrators and remote access only.

extent.notChecked: Systems outside the profiled seven were not checked

gapFindings.consequence: One stolen administrator or vendor password lets ransomware encrypt HIS and Active Directory, which tolerate under four hours of downtime.

likelihood.rationale: MFA is absent on three Criticality A systems, vendor remote access is open, and a peer hospital suffered ransomware.

ops.rationale: Stolen privileged password stops or slows hospital operations.

fin.rationale: Stolen privileged password adds recovery cost and revenue loss.

legal.rationale: Stolen privileged password triggers reporting duties or regulator questions.

rep.rationale: Stolen privileged password damages patient and public trust.

safety.rationale: Stolen privileged password delays or disrupts patient care.

data.rationale: Stolen privileged password exposes sensitive health records.

gapFindings.title: Access is not controlled across the account life cycle
gapFindings.statement: Access rights depend on individuals instead of a governed process, so no one limits, reviews, or removes access consistently.

supportingFacts.fact: No access review ran on HIS, PACS, Microsoft 365, or Active Directory in the past 12 months.
PACS, Active Directory, and the website use shared or generic administrator accounts.
PACS accounts are created on request without approval.
Server room access is only partly restricted and logged.

extent.notChecked: Criticality B systems were not sampled

gapFindings.consequence: Former staff or vendors keep access to patient data unnoticed, and a stolen shared account gives wide reach.

likelihood.rationale: Process gap that needs a leaver or a compromised account before harm.

keyMessage.found: Only PACS has an immutable backup, no restore was tested on critical systems, and the HIS database is not encrypted.
keyMessage.closes: Add offline backups for HIS, ERP, Active Directory, and Microsoft 365, then test a restore.

categories.whatWorksToday: Backups follow a 3-2-1 approach with an immutable PACS copy, and data loss prevention and email authentication are active.

strengths.statement: Data loss prevention detects sensitive data leaving by email, web, or USB.
Email authentication (SPF, DKIM, DMARC) is configured and data loss prevention is active.
Backups follow a 3-2-1 approach, and the PACS backup has an immutable copy.

gapFindings.title: Backups of core systems cannot be shown to survive ransomware
gapFindings.statement: Only the PACS backup has an offline or immutable copy, and no restore test has run on HIS, Microsoft 365, or Active Directory.

supportingFacts.fact: HIS, ERP, and Active Directory back up daily to online storage only.

improvementActions.action: Enforce MFA through the existing Microsoft Entra ID MFA service for all administrator accounts and staff remote access on HIS, PACS, Active Directory, and Microsoft 365.
Require MFA and session logging for vendor remote access and remove unattended remote tools
List every system with its authentication method and MFA status, Criticality A and B first
Approve an authentication standard that requires MFA for new systems
Place systems that cannot support MFA behind a jump host with session logging and a time-limited risk acceptance
Retest MFA on every system that received a Fix and compare the result with the system list from the Find action.
Review MFA coverage each quarter against the system list and record the result with a named owner.
Run a first access review on Criticality A systems, privileged accounts first
Identify shared and generic administrator accounts on PACS, Active Directory, and the website
Link joiner, mover, and leaver steps to HR and set a six-month review cycle
Keep server room access logs and review the access list each quarter
Compare HR leaver records with account lists for the last quarter and confirm that access ended within the agreed time.
Run the access review every six months and file the signed review record.
Record completion of an annual awareness program for all staff
Check the completion records against the staff list and report which staff have not completed the program.
Add an offline or immutable backup copy for HIS, ERP, Active Directory, and Microsoft 365 data
Run and record a restore test on HIS, Microsoft 365, and Active Directory with recovery time measured
Set a restore test schedule for Criticality A systems
Approve a backup standard that requires an offline or immutable copy for every Criticality A system.
Encrypt the HIS database and enforce TLS on all HIS connections
Replace production personal data in test with masked data
Confirm the encryption status of PACS, LIS, and ERP
Scan the HIS test environment for production personal data after masking and record the result.
Check each quarter that new test copies of Criticality A systems use masked data.
Segment the network so HIS, PACS, Active Directory, medical devices, and guest Wi-Fi sit in separate zones with filtered access
Test from the guest Wi-Fi and medical device zones that access to HIS and Active Directory is blocked except by approved rules.
Review the firewall rules between zones every six months and record the review.
Test whether HIS and Active Directory can recover within tolerable downtime
Design a failover or recovery option for the HIS database
Repeat the recovery test on HIS after the failover option is built and compare it with the downtime tolerance.
Test the recovery of Criticality A systems each year and file the exercise report.
Upgrade or isolate the end-of-life PACS platform and the website host
List all systems past end of support with their owners
Set patch timelines by severity and track compliance monthly
Rescan the upgraded or isolated hosts and confirm that no end-of-life software remains.
Isolate legacy medical devices in a dedicated segment and restrict their traffic
Add patching and support terms to medical device vendor contracts
Test that traffic from the medical device segment to other zones is limited to the approved flows.
